coaching.keys: Count the safeties. One high, throw the seam away from the free safety; two high, hunt the hash.
coaching.vsCoverage: Cover 3 dies on the seams. Quarters wants the back or a scramble.
coaching.commentary: Four receivers running vertical stretches every deep defender at once and asks the quarterback one question.

coaching.keys: Read the flat defender. He widens with the back, throw the stick; he sits on the stick, throw the flat.
coaching.commentary: The most-called play in the system. Two defenders, three receivers, and the quarterback only has to be right about one man.

coaching.keys: Off coverage takes the out. Press takes the slant behind it.
The corner is first if the safety is late. Otherwise it is a hitch-flat triangle on the corner.
coaching.commentary: A bunch makes the rub happen without anybody having to run into anybody.

coaching.keys: Off coverage, take the hitch on rhythm. Press or Cover 0, throw the pressed slot vertical.
Shallow to dig, high-low on the middle linebacker. Against man the shallow keeps running.
coaching.commentary: Two in-breaking routes at two depths on one defender. He is wrong either way.

coaching.keys: Corner first against single high. If the flat defender widens, the shallows sit down.
coaching.vsCoverage: Cover 1, run through the mesh. Cover 3, sit at five or six between the hooks.
coaching.commentary: The whole offense in one play: two shallows rubbing, a corner over the top, a swing to the field.

coaching.keys: Post first, then the mandatory fifteen-yard curl, then the wheel up the sideline.
The Texas route by the back is the hot answer against pressure. Everything else is on rhythm.
Under the outside backer, over the Mike, under the weak safety. The ball comes out on time, off the drop.
Find the window between the corner and the flat defender and sit in it.
High-low the corner on both sides. Pick the softer one before the snap and confirm it after.
coaching.commentary: Mirroring the concept means the quarterback never has a wrong side to look at.

coaching.keys: Count the box. If they are light outside, this is a run call that happens to be a throw.
Sell the fade for one step, then work back inside behind the wall.
coaching.commentary: Against a corner who has been beaten deep twice, this is the third-down answer.

coaching.install: Down, down, back. The fullback kicks the end, the backside guard wraps to the playside backer.
coaching.commentary: If the end squeezes, the fullback logs him and the back bounces.

coaching.install: Guard kicks, tackle wraps. The back's first step goes away from the play and sells it.
coaching.commentary: Counter punishes a defense that has learned to chase Power.

coaching.install: The modern spread version: guard and H-back pull instead of guard and tackle.
Let the three-technique come. The backside guard traps him and the back runs off his tail.
coaching.commentary: A penetrating tackle is a gift to a trap team.

coaching.install: The fullback isolates the linebacker in the hole. The back reads that one block and goes.

coaching.keys: Get the ball outside before the edge sets. If the corner squats, crack him and run past.

coaching.install: Both guards pull. The wingback takes it wide behind them.
coaching.commentary: The play the rest of the Buck series exists to set up.

coaching.install: Two double teams, nobody pulls. The back reads the linebacker off the second level.
coaching.commentary: Power's angles without Power's timing risk.

coaching.install: The H-back crosses the formation and whams the three-technique nobody blocked.
The backside tackle pulls and leads through the hole. Cheaper than Power out of an empty backfield.
Down block everything inside, pull the playside guard around the kickout.

coaching.keys: The motion has to be full speed at the snap or the timing is gone.
coaching.commentary: Even when it gains three yards it moves the defense sideways, which is what the rest of the run game wants.

coaching.keys: Read the end man on the line. He chases the sweep, the quarterback keeps it inside behind the pull.
coaching.commentary: The back and the quarterback swap the give and keep roles compared to a normal zone read.

coaching.install: Covered, block him. Uncovered, combo with your neighbour and climb.
coaching.keys: Aiming point is the playside A gap. Press it, then take what the first down lineman gives you.
coaching.commentary: The most-run play in football because it is right against every front without being checked.

coaching.keys: Press the edge until the defense runs with you. The cutback opens up behind their pursuit.

coaching.install: The H-back crosses the formation to kick the backside end, which is the one defender zone rules cannot account for.

coaching.keys: The landmark sits between inside and outside. The back runs a track and takes what the first down lineman gives him.
Leave the backside end unblocked and read him. He crashes, pull it; he sits, give it.
coaching.commentary: Blocking one fewer defender is how a spread offense gets even numbers without an extra tight end.

coaching.install: Covered linemen pin down, uncovered linemen pull around. A zone play with gap-scheme angles.

coaching.keys: Zone blocking with counter backfield action. It is the answer to a fast-flowing linebacker.
Three levels to the boot side. Take the first one that is open and get the ball out.
coaching.commentary: The play the wide zone game is really running toward.

coaching.install: Zone rules on a fullback dive. The option game's answer to a defense that stops the triple.

coaching.keys: The back runs the sweep track and the quarterback keeps it downhill. Roles inverted from a zone read.
The tight end fakes the slice and arcs to the alley instead, which is the read key's tell.
Deep, intermediate, and flat on one side. Whoever the corner and the flat defender cannot both cover is open.
coaching.commentary: Three receivers at three depths against two defenders. One of them comes open every time.

coaching.keys: Two in-breaking routes at different depths. Read the underneath defender's depth and throw off him.
Three receivers in one horizontal band. Throw to the open grass between them.
High-low the corner. If he sinks, throw the hitch; if he squats, throw over him.
The oldest two-man game in the book. The flat defender cannot have both.
The seam clears the safety out of the dig's window. The dig is the throw.
Shallow underneath, basic cross behind it. Against man the shallow wins on the rub.
Same read as the Air Raid version, run out of a pro personnel group.
Fastest answer to pressure in the book. Ball is out on the third step.
Five eligibles, no protection help. The ball has to come out on time or not at all.
Six-yard mesh out of pro personnel. Sit against zone, keep running against man.
Sell the run with the line and the back. The post is only there if the safety bites.
coaching.commentary: Play action works on first and second down, when the defense still has to respect the run.

coaching.keys: Invite the rush, let it go by, and put the ball behind it. Patience is the whole play.
Shallow first against man, dig first against zone. Same play, two answers.
Count the box before the snap. Six defenders on six blockers means hand it off; seven means throw it.
coaching.commentary: The entry-level RPO, and still the one that gets the most yards for the least risk.

coaching.keys: Read the overhang or the down safety. If he fills, the glance is behind him over the linebacker's head.
Punishes a linebacker who triggers downhill on run action. The window is exactly where he left.
Stretch action holds the edge. If the flat defender chases the run, the stick is uncovered.
Gap-scheme action pulls the linebackers hard. The tight end pops into the space they left.
Gap scheme with a perimeter answer. Same pre-snap count, harder run behind it.
Two reads on one snap: the corner's cushion before the ball moves, the end after it.
coaching.commentary: A genuine three-way option out of the gun, and the whole point of storing two reads on one play.

coaching.keys: The read is inverted: it looks like a pass first and the run is the alternative.
Horizontal stress before the snap and vertical stress after it.
Five verticals clear the box out. Everything after that is one man to beat.
If the corner is more than seven yards off, take the free five.
Run call with a downfield peek. If the middle of the field opens, take it; otherwise hand it off.

coaching.install: Read the first man outside the playside tackle for the give. Read the next one for the pitch.
coaching.commentary: Two defenders blocked with two decisions instead of two blockers. That is the whole offense.

coaching.install: The read moves inside to the playside tackle. Answer to a defense widening for the veer.
One read, no pitch. Simpler when the pitch key is unreadable.
The dive track moves outside the tackle and the slot loads the support defender.

coaching.keys: Pre-snap motion, immediate pitch. The fastest way a flexbone gets to the edge.
coaching.commentary: It exists so the defense cannot sit inside waiting for the veer.

coaching.install: Veer action one way, option the other. Punishes a defense that has started to flow.
Answer to a tackle who has learned to crash the dive.
The fullback carries out the dive fake and the quarterback follows him into the same gap.

coaching.keys: Two throws all game, and this is one of them. The safeties have been in the run fit for three quarters.

coaching.install: Straight pitch to the slot without motion. Slower than Rocket, better angles.

coaching.commentary: Once a game, off the look that has already gained forty yards on the ground.
Three fakes before the ball ever goes anywhere. It works because the first two are real plays.

coaching.install: Both guards pull. The wingback takes it wide behind them and the fullback fakes the trap.
coaching.commentary: Everything else in the Buck series is a lie told about this play.

coaching.install: Identical backfield action to the sweep. The fullback keeps it and runs through the trap.

coaching.keys: Three levels away from the sweep flow. The linebackers have already left.
coaching.commentary: The third play of the series, and the one that scores.

coaching.install: Down blocks inside with the wing sealing the edge.
Fullback downhill off the belly fake. The complement to Down.

coaching.keys: Belly fake, then a post-corner combination on a safety who is already downhill.
Full speed at the snap. The motion is the play.

coaching.install: Jet motion pulls the front sideways, the fullback traps back against it.

coaching.commentary: Only works after Buck Sweep has gained ground twice.

coaching.install: The tackle pulls and traps, which nobody scouts for.

coaching.keys: Half the field, three levels, and the quarterback can always run it.
Find the soft spot and sit. Do not drift — the quarterback is throwing to where you stopped.
Ball out on the second step. This is the answer when the rusher is getting home.
coaching.commentary: The single most useful play in a beginner flag playbook.

coaching.keys: The over runner goes first. Settle that in practice so nobody hesitates at the mesh point.
coaching.commentary: In a thirty-yard width two crossers are almost impossible to cover in man.

coaching.keys: One defender, two receivers, two depths. Throw to whichever one he is not covering.
Three verticals against three deep defenders is a footrace, and it takes the whole clock.
coaching.commentary: Only call it with time on the play clock and a quarterback who can get it there.

coaching.keys: Deep, intermediate, shallow, all to one side. Take the open one and get out of bounds.
A stack means nobody can press. The two receivers split one defender vertically.
The two crossers create a natural rub. Order matters: the deeper one clears first.
Sell the corner hard. The safety has to commit before the post breaks back.
Three receivers in a triangle. Against man somebody gets picked without anybody committing one.
The centre is eligible the instant he snaps it. Nobody covers him until you have run this once.
coaching.commentary: Free yards in most youth leagues, and it stays free longer than it should.
Run the hitch three times first. The fourth one is a touchdown.

coaching.keys: The quarterback cannot run it, so the exchange has to be clean and it has to be behind the line.
coaching.commentary: Illegal inside either no-run zone, so check where the ball is spotted before you call it.

coaching.keys: The receiver reads leverage and breaks away from it. Quarterback and receiver have to see the same thing.
A defender who has covered a back all game does not expect him to run vertical.
Inside the five you have to throw it anyway. Put it where only your receiver can get it.
coaching.commentary: The no-run zone makes the goal line a passing situation by rule, so have three of these.

coaching.install: Three deep, four under. The extra man in the box shows up in the run fit, which is the whole reason to play it.
coaching.keys: Corners bail to the deep third at the snap. The curl-flat defenders expand with number two.
coaching.commentary: Vulnerable to four verticals on the seams and to a well-timed flood.

coaching.keys: Man across the board with a free safety in the deep middle and a rat in the hole.
coaching.commentary: Loses to a mesh and to any crossing concept that generates a legal rub.

coaching.keys: Corners squat and re-route number one. Safeties split the field in half.
coaching.commentary: The seam and the deep middle hole are where it dies, which is what Tampa 2 exists to fix.

coaching.keys: The Mike runs the deep middle to about twenty and takes the seam away.
coaching.commentary: Costs you a run defender in the box to buy the middle of the field.

coaching.keys: Played as a pattern match. Safeties become run defenders the moment number two goes flat.
coaching.commentary: Nine in the box against a run and two-high against a pass, if the safeties read it right.

coaching.keys: Five defensive backs against eleven personnel. The nickel plays the curl-flat to the field.
The base call against a spread offense on early downs.
Trail technique underneath with two-deep help over the top.
coaching.commentary: The safest man call, and the one that gives up the most underneath.

coaching.keys: Quarters to the field, Cover 2 to the boundary. Four plus two is six.
coaching.commentary: A hash-dependent call. It stops being clever when the ball is in the middle of the field.

coaching.install: Three down linemen two-gapping so four linebackers can play free.
Stacked linebackers make the front unreadable before the snap.
coaching.commentary: The whole point is that the offense cannot count the box until the ball moves.

coaching.install: Six on the line, everybody in a gap, man behind it.
coaching.commentary: One play-action away from a walk-in touchdown, which is the trade you accept on the two-yard line.

coaching.keys: Five rush, three under, three deep. The end drops into the vacated curl.
coaching.commentary: Pressure without gambling the deep part of the field.

coaching.keys: Both linebackers walk up into the A gaps. Whether they come is decided after the centre declares.
coaching.commentary: Half the value is that the offense has to slide protection before it knows anything.

coaching.keys: The nickel comes off the slot's outside shoulder, which nobody in the protection is assigned to.
Two-high shell before the snap, one-high after it, and the strong safety arrives late.
Everybody not covering somebody is coming. There is no help anywhere.
coaching.commentary: A hot route or a slant beats it every time, so call it when the offense has no time to find one.

coaching.keys: Three deep, everyone else underneath. The base call in most passing leagues.
Two halves over the top. Corners take the flat and re-route the outside receiver.

coaching.commentary: With no rush, man coverage in 7v7 is a test of how long a defender can run.

coaching.keys: One rusher from seven yards, three underneath, one deep.
coaching.commentary: The safest call in flag, and the reason curls and sticks exist.

coaching.keys: Everyone has a man, one safety helps deep. Watch the crossers.
coaching.commentary: Mesh and Quick Cross are designed specifically to beat this.

coaching.keys: Two rushers, everyone else in man with no safety.
coaching.commentary: Quick slants beat it. Call it when the offense has to go deep anyway.

coaching.keys: Nobody rushes. Five defenders cover three receivers and wait for the seven-second clock.
coaching.commentary: The clock is the pass rush. Against a quarterback who holds it, this is a sack every time.
